relearning.title: Read: complex inheritance patterns
relearning.description: A short reading with paint-mixing and checkered-shirt analogies, worked crosses and quick checks.

sections.title: Blends, both and more than two

body.text:
**I can identify complex patterns of inheritance and predict the outcome of complex inheritance crosses.**

Not every trait is simple dominant and recessive. Here are the patterns to know.

**Incomplete dominance: a blend.** Think of mixing red and white paint to get pink. Neither allele fully wins, so the heterozygote is in between. In snapdragons, red (RR) × white (WW) gives all pink (RW).

**Codominance: both show.** Think of a checkered shirt: the red squares and white squares both show, side by side, with no blending. In cattle, red (RR) × white (WW) gives roan (RW), with both red hairs and white hairs.

**Multiple alleles:** blood type has three alleles: A, B and O. A and B are codominant, and O is recessive. AA or AO = type A. BB or BO = type B. AB = type AB. OO = type O.

**Worked example:** Cross two pink snapdragons: RW × RW.

$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & \mathrm{R} & \mathrm{W} \\ \hline \mathrm{R} & \mathrm{RR} & \mathrm{RW} \\ \mathrm{W} & \mathrm{RW} & \mathrm{WW} \end{array}$$

Boxes: 1 RR (red), 2 RW (pink), 1 WW (white). That is 25% red, 50% pink and 25% white. In incomplete dominance, the genotypic and phenotypic ratios match (1:2:1), because each genotype looks different.

checks.prompt: A red snapdragon (RR) is crossed with a white one (WW), and all of the offspring are pink. Which pattern is this?
checks.explanation: Pink is a blend of red and white, so this is incomplete dominance. In codominance both colors would show separately, like red and white patches.

checks.prompt: What percent of the offspring from RW × RW (pink × pink) are expected to be pink? Type a number.
checks.explanation: 2 of the 4 boxes are RW (pink): 50%. Answering 75% is the common mistake: that treats R as dominant, but here only RW is pink.

sections.title: Blood types and sex-linked traits

body.text:
**Worked example 2 (blood type):** A type A parent (AO) and a type B parent (BO) have children.

$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & \mathrm{A} & \mathrm{O} \\ \hline \mathrm{B} & \mathrm{AB} & \mathrm{BO} \\ \mathrm{O} & \mathrm{AO} & \mathrm{OO} \end{array}$$

Boxes: AB, BO, AO and OO, so there is a 25% chance each of type AB, type B, type A and type O. Two parents who aren't type O can still have a type O child.

**Sex-linked traits:** some genes are on the X chromosome. Think of the X as a long book and the Y as a short pamphlet that is missing that page. Females (XX) have two copies of the gene, but males (XY) have only one, so a male with one recessive allele shows the trait. That is why colorblindness and hemophilia are more common in males.

**Worked example 3:** X^{B} = normal vision, X^{b} = colorblind. A carrier mother (X^{B}X^{b}) × a father with normal vision (X^{B}Y). Mom's alleles go across the top, dad's down the side:

$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & \mathrm{X^{B}} & \mathrm{X^{b}} \\ \hline \mathrm{X^{B}} & \mathrm{X^{B}X^{B}} & \mathrm{X^{B}X^{b}} \\ \mathrm{Y} & \mathrm{X^{B}Y} & \mathrm{X^{b}Y} \end{array}$$

Daughters: X^{B}X^{B} and X^{B}X^{b}, so all have normal vision, and half of the daughters are carriers. Sons: X^{B}Y (normal) and X^{b}Y (colorblind), so **50% of the sons** are colorblind. Out of all the children, 1 box of 4 = 25% are colorblind.

**Polygenic traits**, like height and skin color, are controlled by many genes, so they show a smooth range instead of a few types.

**Watch out for:** mixing up incomplete dominance (a blend) and codominance (both show), forgetting that O is recessive (AO is type A), giving a son his X from his dad (sons get their X from mom and their Y from dad), and confusing "50% of the sons" with "50% of all the children."

checks.prompt: Parents with genotypes AO (type A) and BO (type B) have a child. What is the chance the child has type O blood?
checks.explanation: OO is 1 box of 4, so 25%. Answering 0% is the common mistake: neither parent is type O, but each carries an O allele.

checks.prompt: A carrier mother (X^{B}X^{b}) and a father with normal vision (X^{B}Y) have a son. What is the chance he is colorblind?
checks.explanation: A son gets the Y from dad and one of mom's X's: half get X^{B} and half get X^{b}, so 50%. 25% is the chance for all children, not just sons, which is the common mix-up.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain why colorblindness is much more common in males than in females.

relearning.title: Do: work a codominance cross, then a sex-linked cross
relearning.description: Two complex crosses shown one step at a time: roan cattle, then hemophilia.

body.problem: In cattle, red (RR) and white (WW) are codominant: RW cattle are roan, with both red hairs and white hairs. Cross a roan bull with a roan cow. Find the ratios.

steps.text: **Name the pattern:** both colors show in RW, so this is codominance. Use two capital letters and no lowercase.
**Phenotypic ratio:** 1 red : 2 roan : 1 white, or 25% red, 50% roan and 25% white. Each genotype has its own look, so the two ratios match.

checks.prompt: Your turn: black chickens crossed with white chickens give chicks with separate black feathers and white feathers. Which pattern is this?
checks.explanation: Separate black and white feathers means both alleles show: codominance. A blend would give one in-between color, like gray or blue, which is incomplete dominance.

checks.prompt: Your turn: cross a roan (RW) with a white (WW). What percent of the calves are expected to be roan?
checks.explanation: The boxes are RW, WW, RW and WW: 2 of 4 are roan, so 50%. 25% is the answer for RW × RW, the common mix-up.

body.problem: Hemophilia is X-linked recessive. X^{H} = normal clotting, X^{h} = hemophilia. A carrier woman (X^{H}X^{h}) has children with a man who has hemophilia (X^{h}Y). Predict the children.

steps.text: **Parents:** mom is X^{H}X^{h}. Dad is X^{h}Y. Dad has only one X, so his one X^{h} gives him hemophilia.
**Set up the square:** mom's X^{H} and X^{h} go across the top, and dad's X^{h} and Y go down the side.
**Daughters:** X^{H}X^{h} (a carrier with normal clotting) and X^{h}X^{h} (hemophilia). So 50% of the daughters have hemophilia.
**Sons:** X^{H}Y (normal) and X^{h}Y (hemophilia). So 50% of the sons have hemophilia. Out of all the children, 2 boxes of 4 = 50%.

checks.prompt: Your turn: where does a son get his X chromosome?
checks.explanation: A son gets his Y from his father, so his X has to come from his mother. That is why an X-linked trait in a son traces back to his mom.

checks.prompt: Your turn: a woman who is NOT a carrier (X^{H}X^{H}) has children with a man who has hemophilia (X^{h}Y). What percent of their daughters will be carriers?
checks.explanation: Every daughter gets X^{H} from mom and dad's only X, which is X^{h}, so every daughter is X^{H}X^{h}: 100% carriers. The sons get dad's Y, so none of them have hemophilia.

sections.title: Incomplete Dominance, Codominance, Polygenic Traits, and Epistasis!

checks.prompt: In cattle, a red parent (RR) and a white parent (WW) have a roan calf (RW) with both red hairs and white hairs. Which pattern is this?
checks.explanation: Both colors show side by side, like a checkered shirt, so it is codominance. A blend, like pink, would be incomplete dominance, which is the common mix-up.

checks.prompt: Cross a pink snapdragon (RW) with a red snapdragon (RR). What percent of the offspring are expected to be pink?
checks.explanation: The boxes are RR, RW, RR and RW: 2 of 4 are pink, so 50%. None can be white, because the red parent has no W to give.

sections.title: Punnett Squares and Sex-Linked Traits (UPDATED)

checks.prompt: A colorblind father (X^{b}Y) and a mother who is not a carrier (X^{B}X^{B}) have children. What percent of their sons are expected to be colorblind?
checks.explanation: Sons get the Y from dad and their X from mom, and both of mom's X's are X^{B}. Giving a son his X from his dad is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A male has only one X chromosome. What does that mean for an X-linked recessive trait like colorblindness?

options.text: He can be a carrier without showing the trait
One recessive allele is enough for him to show the trait

checks.explanation: The Y is missing that gene, so a male has no second copy to cover a recessive allele. Only females (XX) can be carriers.

sections.shortAnswer: A carrier mother (X^{B}X^{b}) and a colorblind father (X^{b}Y) have a colorblind daughter. Explain where each of her X chromosomes came from and why she is colorblind.

sections.title: Multiple Alleles (ABO Blood Types) and Punnett Squares

checks.prompt: A person with type AB blood has one A allele and one B allele. What does type AB show about the A and B alleles?

options.text: They blend into something in between
They are codominant, so both show

checks.explanation: A and B are codominant: both show, so the blood is type AB. O is the recessive allele. The video may write the alleles as Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i; in class we write A, B and O.

checks.prompt: A type A parent (AO) and a type O parent (OO) have a child. What is the chance the child has type O blood?
checks.explanation: The boxes are AO, AO, OO and OO: 2 of 4 are OO, so 50%. O is recessive, so only OO gives type O; the AO children are type A.
